script_data.title: The World-Changing Error That Launched Modern History
script_data.description: Christopher Columbus sailed west expecting a short route to Asia, but a critical miscalculation of Earth's size led him to stumble upon something far greater! 🌎 How did this single geographical error accidentally reshape global history forever? #HistoryUncovered
script_data.script:
In the late 15th century, Europe pulsed with ambition. The Ottoman Empire's control over traditional Silk Road routes to Asia had choked off the lucrative spice trade, igniting a desperate quest for new sea passages. Amidst this geopolitical fervor emerged an audacious Genoese mariner named Christopher Columbus. Unlike most, Columbus wasn't merely seeking a route; he was convinced he knew the fastest one: west, across the uncharted Atlantic.

His conviction, however, rested on a critical, yet ultimately catastrophic, geographical miscalculation. Columbus largely adopted the ancient Greek geographer Marinus of Tyre's maps, which vastly overestimated the eastward extent of Eurasia, making Asia appear much closer to Europe than it truly was. Compounding this error, he utilized the calculations of Arab astronomer Alfraganus for the Earth's circumference, but applied the shorter Arabic mile instead of the longer Roman mile, effectively shrinking the globe by about 25%. For Columbus, this meant the journey from the Canary Islands to Cipangu (Japan) was a mere 2,400 nautical miles – a manageable distance for his small fleet.

For years, learned scholars across Europe, notably the Junta de Cosmógrafos in Salamanca, scoffed at his proposals, accurately arguing that his estimated distance was dangerously short and the true voyage impossible with the provisions of the time. But Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, finally victorious in the Reconquista and eager to challenge Portugal's maritime dominance, finally gambled on his "Enterprise of the Indies."

On August 3, 1492, Columbus set sail from Palos de la Frontera with the *Niña*, *Pinta*, and *Santa María*. The voyage was arduous, the crew growing increasingly mutinous as weeks turned into months, far exceeding Columbus's projected timeframe. His erroneous calculations meant they should have reached Asia long ago. Just as hope dwindled, on October 12, 1492, land was sighted. Columbus, believing he had skirted the eastern coast of Asia, confidently named the inhabitants "Indians."

He was profoundly mistaken. Instead of the bustling ports of Cathay or the spice islands of the Indies, he had stumbled upon an entirely unknown hemisphere – the Americas. His "minor" miscalculation wasn't minor at all; it was a colossal error that inadvertently repositioned the entire world. This single geographical blunder didn't just open a new trade route; it unveiled two continents, triggering centuries of European colonization, the horrific transatlantic slave trade, the Columbian Exchange of plants, animals, and diseases, and the explosive growth of global trade networks that irrevocably reshaped human civilization and economics on every continent. The modern world, with all its interconnected complexities, was, in essence, accidentally discovered.

script_data.used_topic_seed: Christopher Columbus, driven by ambition and a critical but flawed understanding of Earth's size, chose to sail west expecting a short route to Asia. This seemingly minor miscalculation of global geography led him to accidentally encounter the Americas, triggering centuries of European colonization, global trade, and reshaping the course of human history.
